column3: A direct source-language parallel: compassion and purity are granted from God's nearness.
Begins Moses's journey to the servant whose divinely granted knowledge is introduced at the focus.
Shares the plea for a gift from God's nearness, but its requested heir is unrelated to special knowledge.
Directly pairs mercy from Us with a servant of God, closely matching the focus's granted mercy.
The servant later explains the first act of hidden wisdom introduced by the focus.
Combines God's servants with His comprehensive knowledge, but concerns provision rather than granted instruction.
Closely parallels mercy from God's nearness and its guidance-giving effect within the same surah.
Continues the journey that immediately leads Moses to the divinely taught servant.
Shares a gift from God's nearness but speaks of reward, not mercy or knowledge.
Calls the prophets believing servants of God, supporting the focus's dependent servant identity.
The servant later explains his second action as protective knowledge and mercy.
God's favor and knowledge resonate generally, without the focus's granted-teaching pattern.
A clear parallel in which God grants judgment and knowledge to a chosen person.
Advances the journey immediately preceding the encounter with the servant.
A gift from God's nearness is reward for deeds, not the focus's mercy and knowledge.
Describes Abraham as one of God's believing servants, a general parallel to the focus's servant identity.
The servant's intended replacement is explicitly described as nearer in mercy, explaining the focus's granted mercy in action.
Contrasts unsupported worship with knowledge and authority, indirectly clarifying the focus's God-given knowledge.
Describes Elijah as one of God's believing servants, a general servant-status parallel.
The lost fish sign turns the travelers back toward the servant identified in the focus.
Within the same surah, God's mercy and guidance are sought by people who withdraw for faithful worship.
Describes Noah as one of God's believing servants, supporting the dependent servant designation.
The servant attributes his acts to mercy from the Lord and denies acting on his own command, directly explaining the focus's dependent authority.
Uses from Our nearness in a distinct hypothetical claim, without mercy or teaching.
God grants David and Solomon knowledge, closely paralleling the focus's bestowed knowledge.
Moses and his companion retrace their steps to the encounter in the focus.
Restricts understanding to the learned, but does not identify knowledge as divinely granted to a servant.
A contrary example of inherited worship that sharpens the focus's exclusive divine servanthood.
Moses asks to follow the servant so he may learn from what the servant was taught, the immediate continuation of the focus.
Exclusive worship of God supports the servant's defining relation, though not the mercy-and-knowledge grant.
God grants Moses judgment and knowledge, a close counterpart to the focus's teaching.
The servant states Moses cannot patiently endure what he lacks knowledge of, developing the focus's special knowledge.
A reminder is given from God's nearness, paralleling revelation as a divine gift of knowledge.
Identifies a divine favor from Us, though not the focus's specific mercy or knowledge.
Explicitly links Moses's lack of encompassing knowledge to his inability to endure the servant's acts.
Discusses worshipers and what they worship, a general contrast that reinforces true servanthood.
God's servants and piety overlap, but the verse concerns inheritance of Paradise.
Moses pledges patience and obedience in response to the servant's special teaching.
Punishment and ignorance do not clarify the focus's mercy, servanthood, or granted knowledge.
A near-verbatim parallel requesting mercy from God's nearness.
Sets the conditions under which Moses may follow the divinely taught servant.
Revelation is sent with God's knowledge, supporting divine knowledge as the source of disclosed teaching.
A wish for earlier remembrance is only a distant parallel to divine teaching.
Repeats the servant's warning about Moses's inability to endure knowledge he does not encompass.
The Quran is received from the presence of the Wise, Knowing One, closely paralleling source-given knowledge.
God grants Lot judgment and knowledge, a direct analogue to the focus's bestowed knowledge.
Moses's plea after forgetfulness develops the learning relationship established at the focus.
Addresses God's believing servants and commands exclusive worship, supporting the servant identity.
Noah is called a grateful servant, a general positive parallel to the focus's servant designation.
Again foregrounds Moses's inability to bear the servant's hidden knowledge.
God's knowledge of concealed and open matters is broad but does not concern a granted human knowledge.
Chosen excellence before God is a distant status parallel without mercy or teaching.
The servant ends companionship after Moses's questions, showing the boundary around the teaching.
Knowledge of revealed limits is a loose parallel and its social setting is unrelated.
Truth comes from Us, a source-language parallel without the focus's teaching and mercy.
The wall-repair episode becomes one of the acts explained as mercy and non-self-directed action.
Defers disputed knowledge to the Lord in the same surah, supporting epistemic dependence.
Uses servant for one at prayer, supporting the basic devotional sense of the focus's designation.
The servant promises the interpretation of what Moses could not bear, directly unpacking his special knowledge.
God clarifies what people must heed, a general divine-teaching parallel.
God teaches David a craft, showing practical knowledge bestowed by divine instruction.
The first apparently troubling act whose hidden rationale is later disclosed by the servant.
Explicitly marks the limit of human knowledge, sharpening the focus's contrast between granted and comprehensive knowledge.
All beings come to the Merciful as servants, broadening the focus's servant identity.
The second troubling act that the servant later explains through hidden knowledge and mercy.
Future knowing is not a close parallel to the focus's present divine instruction.
Provision from Us and lack of knowledge share wording but not the focus's teaching.
Requests a protector and helper from God's nearness, but not mercy or knowledge.
The owned servant image contrasts human incapacity with divinely given provision, indirectly supporting dependent status.
Deferred knowledge after heedless enjoyment does not clarify the focus's special teaching.
Mercy from the Lord is joined to His hearing and knowledge, a close divine-source parallel.
Self-knowledge at judgment is unrelated to the bestowed mercy and instruction at the focus.
Someone given God's signs abandons them, a contrast to faithful reception of divine knowledge.
Future knowledge following distraction is only a remote thematic parallel.
Affirms that even Christ and the near angels do not disdain being servants of God, strongly illuminating the focus's servanthood.
Human knowledge can fade with age, a broad contrast to divinely granted knowledge.
God knows all while creatures cannot encompass His knowledge, directly framing the limit behind the focus's received knowledge.
God knows the unseen and deeds, a broad source-of-knowledge parallel.
God encompasses all things in knowledge, contrasting comprehensive divine knowledge with the servant's received share.
A repeated warning of future knowledge adds little to the focus's divine teaching.
Rebukes people for denying signs without encompassing them in knowledge, a contrast to humble learning.
Commands worship and God-consciousness, supporting the focus's servant relation in a general way.
God's mercy and sole protection are relevant generally but not to teaching or the servant's role.
The news of a knowledgeable child is not a close source or teaching parallel.
Commands the Prophet to seek increase in knowledge while receiving revelation, a close model of divinely sourced learning.
States that jinn and humankind were created to worship God, grounding the focus's servant identity.
God's knowledge of human limits moderates worship obligations, a broad mercy-and-knowledge resonance.
God's hearing and knowledge support seeking refuge, but not the focus's granted knowledge.
Good deeds found with God do not clarify the focus's mercy or instruction.
God's witness distinguishes true worship from claims about it, indirectly supporting rightful servanthood.
Reward from God is a different kind of divine giving from the focus's mercy and knowledge.
Forbids speaking about God without knowledge, a cautionary but indirect parallel.
A messenger recites clear signs to bring believers into light, a general mediated-teaching parallel.
God teaches the Quran, strongly affirming divine teaching though without the focus's servant-and-mercy setting.
God's all-encompassing knowledge and the limited knowledge granted by His will directly frame the focus's received knowledge.
The messenger teaches what people did not know, a close human-facing instance of divinely provided instruction.
A blessed greeting from God has only a lexical source-language overlap.
Moses's mission from the Lord is narrative context but does not clarify the servant's mercy or knowledge.
Self-sufficiency contrasts loosely with dependent servanthood, without a direct knowledge or mercy link.
Misleading God's servants is a broad contrast but adds little to the focus's specific themes.
God teaches Adam the names, a foundational instance of human knowledge explicitly given by God.
The angels confess that they know only what God has taught them, directly framing received knowledge as dependent.
Talut is chosen with an increase in knowledge from God, paralleling divinely bestowed capacity.
God gives wisdom to whomever He wills, a compact general parallel to the focus's granted knowledge.
God promises to teach Jesus the Book and wisdom, an explicit divine-teaching parallel.
Teaching and studying the Book grounds devoted servants of God, joining learning with servant identity.
The messenger's recitation, purification, and teaching show divine guidance reaching people through instruction.
God teaches the Prophet the Book and wisdom and describes His favor as immense.
Those firmly grounded in knowledge receive and affirm revelation, a receptive counterpart to given knowledge.
God teaches Jesus the Book, wisdom, Torah, and Gospel, closely paralleling bestowed instruction.
God gives chosen people the Book, judgment, and prophethood, a strong grant-of-guidance parallel.
A Book detailed with knowledge is described as guidance and mercy, joining the focus's two gifts.
The tablets contain guidance and mercy for those who fear their Lord, a revelation-and-mercy parallel.
God teaches Joseph the interpretation of events, a direct narrative parallel to special granted knowledge.
God teaches Joseph the interpretation of events, again identifying such knowledge as divine instruction.
Joseph explicitly says that his Lord taught him, directly matching the focus's passive reception of knowledge.
Jacob possesses knowledge because God taught him, one of the clearest parallels to the focus's wording and claim.
God brings people forth knowing nothing and gives the faculties through which knowledge is received.
The Quran is sent down as healing and mercy, a direct divine-mercy counterpart to the focus.
Humans are given only a little knowledge, directly delimiting creaturely knowledge beside the focus's special gift.
The Lord is full of mercy and does not hasten punishment, supplying the surah's broader mercy frame.
God's words cannot be exhausted, strongly contrasting divine knowledge with finite human reception.
God gives Abraham sound judgment and knows him, a close precedent for divinely granted discernment.
God grants Solomon understanding and gives both David and Solomon judgment and knowledge.
Those given knowledge recognize revelation as truth from their Lord, a reception-side parallel to divine teaching.
Abraham asks his Lord to grant him wisdom, a direct prayer for the kind of God-given understanding at issue.
Solomon declares that he has been taught the language of birds, an explicit bestowed-teaching parallel.
A person with knowledge from the Book acts with exceptional capacity, echoing knowledge granted from a divine source.
Clear signs reside in the hearts of those given knowledge, linking revelation to a recipient community of learning.
Those given knowledge recognize what was revealed as truth and guidance, a related response to divine disclosure.
Those who truly fear God are described as the knowledgeable among His servants, joining knowledge and servanthood.
God gives David wisdom and decisive judgment, another direct instance of divinely granted intellectual authority.
Contrasts those who know with those who do not, while linking knowledge to devoted worship.
Revelation is called a spirit from God's command; the Prophet had not known the Book or faith until God made it guiding light.
God gives the Children of Israel the Book, judgment, and prophethood, a collective parallel to bestowed guidance and knowledge.
The messenger says knowledge is only with God and that he merely conveys what he is sent with, marking dependent authority.
God raises those who believe and are given knowledge, affirming knowledge as a granted and honored status.
The messenger recites signs, purifies, and teaches the Book and wisdom to those previously in clear error.
God takes responsibility for explaining the Quran, an explicit source-of-teaching parallel.
God promises to teach the Prophet the recitation so that he will not forget, a direct instructional grant.
God teaches by the pen, a foundational statement of divine teaching.
God teaches the human being what he did not know, one of the closest general parallels to the focus.
